claim: Huntington's disease is caused by the expansion of a CAG repeat in the open-reading frame of the huntingtin gene (HTT), which translates into an expanded glutamine stretch in the aberrant, mutant protein (mHTT).
source: Huntington's disease is caused by the expansion of a CAG repeat in the open-reading frame of the huntingtin gene (HTT), which translates into an expanded glutamine stretch in the aberrant, mutant protein (mHTT).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the genetic basis of Huntington's disease.

claim: Huntington's disease has primarily been described as a late-onset neurodegenerative disease.
source: Huntington's disease has primarily been described as a late-onset neurodegenerative disease.
evidence: This is a statement about how Huntington's disease has been characterized in the literature.

claim: Huntington's disease is preceded in its premanifest period by a prolonged presymptomatic phase followed by a prodromal phase with hardly detectable and unspecific symptoms occurring far before classical Huntington's disease becomes apparent.
source: However, it is preceded in its premanifest period by a prolonged presymptomatic phase followed by a prodromal phase with hardly detectable and unspecific symptoms occurring far before classical Huntington's disease becomes apparent (Ross et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ross et al., 2014.

claim: Premanifest Huntington's disease symptoms include reduced impulse control, social disengagement, low conversational participation, reduction of the concentration span and decline of clearly defined cognitive domains.
source: These symptoms include reduced impulse control, social disengagement, low conversational participation, reduction of the concentration span and decline of clearly defined cognitive domains (Stout et al., 2011; Predict-HD Investigators of the Huntington Study Group et al., 2007; Ross et al., 2014; Labuschagne et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Premanifest Huntington's disease symptoms are accompanied by slight changes of cortical network topology and functional connectivity in resting state fMRI measures.
source: and are accompanied by slight changes of cortical network topology and functional connectivity in resting state fMRI measures (PREDICT-HD investigators of the Huntington Study Group et al., 2015; Wolf et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to fMRI studies.

claim: Subtle network dysregulations may occur even earlier than the described prodromal symptoms in a very far from disease onset (VFDO) premanifest stage.
source: Importantly, such subtle network dysregulations may occur even earlier than the described prodromal symptoms in a very far from disease onset (VFDO) premanifest stage (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1a which illustrates the timeline of disease progression.

claim: The VFDO stage reaches back more than 15–20 years before motor symptoms become visible in patients and far before protein aggregates and neurodegeneration are observed.
source: This stage reaches back more than 15–20 years before motor symptoms become visible in patients and far before protein aggregates and neurodegeneration are observed.
evidence: This is a temporal characterization of the VFDO stage based on the timeline shown in Figure 1.

claim: Early deficits in premanifest Huntington's disease mutation carriers include loss of phosphodiesterase 10A in the occipital lobe up to 47 years prior to disease onset.
source: In Huntington's disease occurrence of such very early changes is supported by the observation of early deficits in premanifest Huntington's disease mutation carriers, such as loss of phosphodiesterase 10A in the occipital lobe up to 47 years prior to disease onset (summarized in Wilson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wilson et al., 2017.

claim: The ability to perform complex visuospatial orientation, such as visual search, seems to be altered even in pre-manifest stages far from clinical diagnosis.
source: Also, the ability to perform complex visuospatial orientation, such as visual search, seems to be altered even in pre-manifest stages far from clinical diagnosis (Labuschagne et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Labuschagne et al., 2016.

claim: Primal functional changes in the VFDO stage of premanifest Huntington's disease open up very early vulnerable windows for disease development and preventive therapy prior to neuronal loss.
source: We hypothesize that primal functional changes in the VFDO stage of premanifest Huntington's disease open up very early vulnerable windows for disease development and preventive therapy prior to neuronal loss and may also provide promising early biomarkers for therapy development (Mehler and Gokhan, 2000; Kerschbamer and Biagioli, 2015; Humbert, 2010; Cepeda et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: The visual cortex is one of the first regions that are functionally affected during disease development in Huntington's disease.
source: It seems that the visual cortex is one of the first regions that are functionally affected during disease development in Huntington's disease (Labuschagne et al., 2016; Dogan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on visual cortex function in Huntington's disease.

claim: At the early age of 10-15 weeks in Hdh150 mice, the entire cortical microcircuit shifts towards a more excitable state characterized by a complex change in neuronal activity pattern and hyperactive neurons.
source: We show that even at the early age of 10 – 15 weeks (young adults compared to humans), the entire cortical microcircuit shifts towards a more excitable state characterized by a complex change in neuronal activity pattern and hyperactive neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Early network changes in Hdh150 mice are accompanied by changes in animal behavior, including a decrease in anxiety.
source: These findings are accompanied by changes in animal behavior, including a decrease in anxiety.
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Short-term reduction of protein load through RNA interference and antisense strategies has beneficial effects on disease phenotypes and progression lasting several months after intervention in Huntington's disease animal models.
source: In Huntington's disease animal models, even short-term reduction of protein load through RNA interference and antisense strategies has beneficial effects on disease phenotypes and progression lasting several months after intervention (Stanek et al., 2014; DiFiglia et al., 2007; Keiser et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on RNA interference and antisense strategies.

claim: mRNAs carrying CAG repeats bind to a protein complex containing the ubiquitin ligase midline 1 (MID1) in a repeat size-dependent manner.
source: We have recently shown that mRNAs carrying CAG repeats bind to a protein complex containing the ubiquitin ligase midline 1 (MID1) in a repeat size-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors.

claim: Through ubiquitination MID1 regulates PP2A (protein phosphatase 2A) and mTOR (mechanistic target of rapamycin) activities and the translation of associated mRNAs.
source: Through ubiquitination MID1 regulates PP2A (protein phosphatase 2A) and mTOR (mechanistic target of rapamycin) activities and the translation of associated mRNAs (Krauss et al., 2013; Griesche et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Disruption of the MID1/PP2A/mTOR protein complex leads to an increase of PP2A activity, a decrease of mTOR activity and a reduction of translation rates of mRNAs with expanded CAG repeats.
source: Disruption of the MID1/PP2A/mTOR protein complex leads to an increase of PP2A activity, a decrease of mTOR activity and a reduction of translation rates of mRNAs with expanded CAG repeats (Krauss et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Metformin interferes with the MID1/PP2A/mTOR protein complex and significantly reduces the translation rate of Htt mRNA, resulting in a reduction of aberrant Htt protein production in vitro and in vivo in the Hdh150 mouse model.
source: We show here that the type II diabetes drug metformin interferes with the MID1/PP2A/mTOR protein complex and significantly reduces the translation rate of Htt mRNA, resulting in a reduction of aberrant Htt protein production in vitro and in vivo in the Hdh150 mouse model.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: In Hdh150 mice in vivo metformin, when given early in the VFDO stage, and chronically in the drinking water, fully reverses both early neuronal network dysregulations and behavioral aberrations.
source: Notably, in Hdh150 mice in vivo metformin, when given early in the VFDO stage, and chronically in the drinking water, fully reverses both early neuronal network dysregulations and behavioral aberrations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: The study focused on layer 2/3 of the visual cortex of ~12 weeks old, heterozygous knock-in mice expressing expanded Htt with 150 glutamine repeats (Hdh150), in the lightly anesthetized mouse.
source: Since the visual cortex is one of the first regions affected by the disease (Dogan et al., 2013; Labuschagne et al., 2016), we focused on layer 2/3 of the visual cortex of ∼12 weeks old, heterozygous knock-in mice expressing expanded Htt with 150 glutamine repeats (Hdh150), in the lightly anesthetized mouse.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The study employed two-photon Ca2+ imaging in vivo using the synthetic Ca2+ indicator Oregon-Green BAPTA1 (OGB-1) AM to monitor the suprathreshold activity of a neuronal microcircuit with cellular resolution.
source: We employed two-photon Ca2+ imaging in vivo using the synthetic Ca2+ indicator Oregon-Green BAPTA1 (OGB-1) AM to monitor the suprathreshold activity of a neuronal microcircuit with cellular resolution, typically comprising around 200 neurons (Kerr et al., 2005) (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: There was no difference in the density of stained cells between Hdh150 and control wild-type (WT) mice.
source: We observed no difference in the density of stained cells (Figure 1c and e, Figure 1—source data 1, WT: 1413 ± 74 cells/mm2 (n = 11 mice), Hdh150 1456 ± 90 cells/mm2 (n = 10 mice), Mann-Whitney test p=0.8).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: A significantly higher proportion of active neurons was detected in Hdh150 mice compared to WT mice, indicating a more active network.
source: Both WT and Hdh150 mice exhibited silent and active cells (Figure 1d), but a significantly higher proportion of active neurons was detected in Hdh150 mice, indicating a more active network (Figure 1f, Figure 1—source data 1, WT: 65.1 ± 3.5% (n = 8 mice), Hdh150: 77.1 ± 3.5% (n = 6 mice), unpaired t-test p<0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The frequency of Ca2+ transients was significantly higher in Hdh150 compared to WT mice.
source: Notably, the frequency of Ca2+ transients was significantly higher in Hdh150 compared to WT mice (Figure 1g–h, Figure 1—source data 1, WT: 0.74 ± 0.06 trans/min (n = 8 mice), Hdh150: 1.2 ± 0.14 trans/min (n = 6 mice), Mann-Whitney test, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: No difference was found in the mean area under the curve (AUC) of Ca2+ transients between WT and Hdh150 mice.
source: No difference was found in the mean area under the curve (AUC) of Ca2+ transients between WT and Hdh150 mice (Figure 1i, Figure 1—source data 1, WT: 39.8 ± 3.9 (dF/f)*s, Hdh150: 39.9 ± 3.6 (dF/f)*s, unpaired t-test, p=0.98)
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The mean number of underlying action potentials for each individual calcium transient was not different in Hdh150 mice.
source: indicating that on average, the mean number of underlying action potentials for each individual calcium transient was not different in Hdh150 mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the AUC data.

claim: The cumulative probability distribution of the activity of individual neurons in Huntington's disease mice was shifted toward higher frequencies indicating that the overall neuronal activity transitioned toward a more excitable network.
source: The cumulative probability distribution of the activity of individual neurons in Huntington's disease mice was shifted toward higher frequencies indicating that the overall neuronal activity transitioned toward a more excitable network (Figure 1j, Figure 1—source data 1, two-way ANOVA p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: A unique subgroup of hyperactive neurons was identified in VFDO Hdh150 mice.
source: Notably, we identified a unique subgroup in VFDO Hdh150 mice: hyperactive neurons (Figure 1l, Figure 1—source data 1, Chi-square test p<0.01).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The hyperactive subgroup was accompanied by a reduction in the number of neurons with low activity.
source: This subgroup was accompanied by a reduction in the number of neurons with low activity, which corroborates the shift of the microcircuit activity.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Only diffuse and non-aggregated Htt immunoreactivity was observed in the cytoplasm of neurons in cortical areas of both WT and Hdh150 mice.
source: We observed only diffuse and non-aggregated Htt immunoreactivity in the cytoplasm of neurons in cortical areas of both WT and Hdh150 mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a) in accordance with previous studies (Lin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry experiments, supported by a citation.

claim: No reactive astrocytes were observed in cortical areas of WT and Hdh150 mice.
source: In addition, no reactive astrocytes were observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b)
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry experiments.

claim: Only few cells were stained for activated caspase-3, an apoptotic marker, in cortical areas of WT and Hdh150 mice.
source: and only few cells that were stained for activated caspase-3, an apoptotic marker, in cortical areas of WT and Hdh150 mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c) as previously observed (Yu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemistry experiments, supported by a citation.

claim: No significant differences were observed between the permutations of functional subgroups in premanifest Hdh150 and control mice, reflecting a rather homogenous distribution of all functional subgroups.
source: We observed no significant differences between the permutations of functional subgroups in premanifest Hdh150 and control mice, reflecting a rather homogenous distribution of all functional subgroups (Figure 1—figure supplement 3c,d, Figure 1—source data 1, Mann-Whitney, not significant, see Table 1 for p-values).
evidence: This is a finding from spatial analysis of the data, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Clustering of hyperactive cells could not be observed in VFDO Hdh150 animals.
source: Taken together, clustering of hyperactive cells could not be observed in VFDO Hdh150 animals
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the spatial analysis data.

claim: Cortical hyperactivity is independent of mHtt aggregation, apoptotic cell death or astrogliosis at the presymptomatic VFDO stage.
source: and cortical hyperactivity is independent of mHtt aggregation, apoptotic cell death or astrogliosis at this presymptomatic VFDO stage.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the immunohistochemistry and spatial analysis data.

claim: The level of synchronicity within a healthy cortical microcircuit is drastically higher than the random synchronicity in shuffled data.
source: First, we confirmed that the level of synchronicity within a healthy cortical microcircuit is drastically higher than the random synchronicity in shuffled data (Figure 2b, Figure 2—source data 1, WT: 0.024 ± 0.005, WT rand: −0.0003 ± 0.0003, Mann-Whitney test p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from the synchronicity analysis, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The synchronicity was even higher in Hdh150 mice compared to healthy controls.
source: Notably, the synchronicity was even higher in Hdh150 mice compared to healthy controls (Figure 2b, Figure 2—source data 1, WT: 0.02 ± 0.005, Hdh150: 0.04 ± 0.006, Mann-Whitney test p<0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the synchronicity analysis, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The pairs involving the low activity subgroups (LL and LM) showed no differences in WT and Hdh150 mice.
source: The pairs involving the low activity subgroups (LL and LM) showed no differences in WT and Hdh150 mice (Mann-Whitney test, in LL p=0.5 and in LM p=0.7).
evidence: This is a finding from the synchronicity analysis, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Pearson's r increased significantly for the medium-to-medium (MM) pairs in Hdh150.
source: However, Pearson's r increased significantly for the medium-to-medium (MM) pairs in Hdh150.
evidence: This is a finding from the synchronicity analysis.

claim: Pearson's r was even higher for medium-hyperactive (MH) and hyperactive-hyperactive (HH) compared to low-low (LL) pairs in Hdh150 mice.
source: Pearson's r was even higher for medium-hyperactive (MH) and hyperactive-hyperactive (HH) compared to low-low (LL) pairs (Mann-Whitney test compared to LL in Hdh150 mice: in MM p<0.05, in MH and HH p<0.01).
evidence: This is a finding from the synchronicity analysis, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Pearson's r in the randomized data was nearly zero for all, including the high frequency subgroups in WT and Hdh150 mice.
source: Pearson's r in the randomized data was nearly zero for all, including the high frequency subgroups in WT and Hdh150 mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and b, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the randomized data analysis.

claim: The increased Pearson's r in the experimental data did not occur by chance.
source: This finding argued against the possibility that the increased Pearson's r in the experimental data occurred by chance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the randomized data analysis.

claim: An inverse linear relationship was observed between Pearson's r and the pairwise distance in both the WT and Hdh150 mice.
source: An inverse linear relationship was observed between Pearson's r and the pairwise distance in both the WT and Hdh150 mice (Figure 2d, Figure 2—source data 1, two-way ANOVA p<0.0001, WT vs Hdh150)
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Two closely located neurons have a higher probability to fire together.
source: suggesting that two closely located neurons have a higher probability to fire together.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inverse relationship between Pearson's r and distance.

claim: This finding is consistent with similar findings in the forelimb motor cortex of head-restrained mice.
source: This is consistent with similar findings in the forelimb motor cortex of head-restrained mice (Dombeck et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous findings, supported by a citation.

claim: Randomization of the data abolished the inverse relationship between Pearson's r and distance.
source: Randomization of the data abolished the inverse relationship between Pearson's r and distance (Figure 2e, Figure 2—source data 1, two-way ANOVA p=0.3, WT rand vs Hdh150 rand).
evidence: This is a finding from the randomized data analysis, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Mitochondrial respiration was unchanged in cortical tissue of Hdh150 mice.
source: Mitochondrial respiration was unchanged in cortical tissue of Hdh150 mice suggesting that the observed neuronal hyperactivity occurs prior to metabolic changes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–c, Figure 2—source data 1, Mann-Whitney test, not significant, see Table 1 for p-values).
evidence: This is a finding from the mitochondrial respiration assay, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The observed neuronal hyperactivity occurs prior to metabolic changes.
source: suggesting that the observed neuronal hyperactivity occurs prior to metabolic changes
evidence: This is an inference based on the mitochondrial respiration data.

claim: A visual discrimination task did not show any aberrations in the Hdh150 animals.
source: A visual discrimination task did not show any aberrations in the Hdh150 animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–d; Figure 3—video 1, Figure 3—source data 1, two-way ANOVA, not significant, see Table 1 for p-values).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral experiments, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: In an open-field test premanifest VDFO Hdh150 animals moved significantly more to the center than WT littermates suggesting anxiolytic effects of the VFDO changes.
source: In contrast, in an open-field test premanifest VDFO Hdh150 animals moved significantly more to the center than WT littermates suggesting anxiolytic effects of the VFDO changes (Figure 3a,b, Figure 3—source data 1, Mann-Whitney test, p=0.03).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral experiments, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Distance travelled (as a measure of motility) did not differ between groups.
source: Distance travelled (as a measure of motility) did not differ between groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e, Figure 3—source data 1, Mann-Whitney test, not significant, see Table 1 for p-values).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral experiments, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Metformin reduced the amount of aggregated FLAG-HTT in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Metformin reduced the amount of aggregated FLAG-HTT in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 4a, Figure 4—source data 1, Mann-Whitney test, control vs 2.5 mM metformin p=0.02).
evidence: This is a finding from the filter retardation assay, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Depletion of MID1 reduced mHTT aggregation.
source: While depletion of MID1 reduced mHTT aggregation, no additive effect of metformin treatment on mHTT aggregates was observed, suggesting that MID1 and metformin indeed act through the same pathway (Figure 4b, Figure 4—source data 1, Mann-Whitney test, control siRNA vs MID1 siRNA p=0.009; control siRNA vs MID1 siRNA +metformin p=0.02).
evidence: This is a finding from the siRNA knockdown experiment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: No additive effect of metformin treatment on mHTT aggregates was observed when MID1 was depleted, suggesting that MID1 and metformin indeed act through the same pathway.
source: While depletion of MID1 reduced mHTT aggregation, no additive effect of metformin treatment on mHTT aggregates was observed, suggesting that MID1 and metformin indeed act through the same pathway (Figure 4b, Figure 4—source data 1, Mann-Whitney test, control siRNA vs MID1 siRNA p=0.009; control siRNA vs MID1 siRNA +metformin p=0.02).
evidence: This is an inference based on the siRNA knockdown experiment data.

claim: A clear reduction in the protein synthesis rate of a GFP-Htt fusion protein carrying 49 repeats was detected in the metformin-treated samples in a concentration-dependent manner in primary neurons.
source: We detected a clear reduction in the protein synthesis rate of a GFP-Htt fusion protein carrying 49 repeats in the metformin-treated samples in a concentration-dependent manner in primary neurons (Figure 4c, Figure 4—source data 1, RM two-way ANOVA p=0.008).
evidence: This is a finding from the FRAP-based assay, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: This effect was confirmed in N2A cells.
source: This effect was confirmed in N2A cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, Figure 4—source data 1, RM two-way ANOVA p=0.03).
evidence: This is a finding from the FRAP-based assay in N2A cells, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: OA significantly increased translation rates of the GFP-Htt reporter mRNA.
source: As expected, OA significantly increased translation rates of the GFP-Htt reporter mRNA
evidence: This is a finding from the FRAP-based assay with OA treatment.

claim: Metformin did not have a reducing effect on the translation rates in cells co-treated with OA suggesting that indeed the metformin effect is mediated by PP2A activity.
source: and metformin did not have a reducing effect on the translation rates in cells co-treated with OA suggesting that indeed the metformin effect is mediated by PP2A activity (Figure 4d, Figure 4—source data 1, RM two-way ANOVA p=0.002).
evidence: This is an inference based on the FRAP-based assay with OA and metformin co-treatment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Metformin did not significantly reduce drinking volume in Hdh150 mice.
source: Metformin did not significantly reduce drinking volume (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b, Figure 4—source data 1, RM two-way ANOVA not significant, see Table 1 for p-values).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo metformin treatment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The metformin-treated group showed a significant reduction of S6 phosphorylation suggesting an increase in PP2A activity.
source: The metformin-treated group showed a significant reduction of S6 phosphorylation suggesting an increase in PP2A activity (Figure 4e and f, Figure 4—source data 1, unpaired t-test p=0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the western blot analysis, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: A slight tendency (not significant) of reduced mHtt was detected after 3 weeks of metformin treatment suggesting that metformin has an influence on mHtt expression.
source: At the same time, a slight tendency (not significant) of reduced mHtt was detected suggesting that metformin has an influence on mHtt expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c and d, Figure 4—source data 1, unpaired t-test not significant, see Table 1 for p-values).
evidence: This is a finding from the western blot analysis after 3 weeks of treatment.

claim: A significant reduction of mHtt expression became clearly visible after 11 weeks of treatment in cortical tissue.
source: A significant reduction of mHtt expression, however, became clearly visible after 11 weeks of treatment in cortical tissue (Figure 4g–j, Figure 4—source data 1, unpaired t-test, mHtt/wtHtt p=0.05, mHtt/Gapdh p=0.002, wtHtt/Gapdh p=0.9).
evidence: This is a finding from the western blot analysis after 11 weeks of treatment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: 5 days of metformin treatment reduced the number of intracellular inclusion bodies significantly in C. elegans.
source: We found that 5 days of metformin treatment reduced the number of intracellular inclusion bodies significantly and rescued motility impairment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a and b, Figure 4—source data 1, Mann-Whitney, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from the C. elegans experiments, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: 5 days of metformin treatment rescued motility impairment in C. elegans.
source: We found that 5 days of metformin treatment reduced the number of intracellular inclusion bodies significantly and rescued motility impairment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a and b, Figure 4—source data 1, Mann-Whitney, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from the C. elegans experiments, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The metformin effect on inclusion bodies was confirmed on heat-inactivated OP50 bacteria.
source: Since bacteria can metabolize metformin (Cabreiro et al., 2013), we confirmed the results on heat-inactivated OP50 bacteria (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c, Figure 4—source data 1, Mann-Whitney test, control vs 5 mM metformin p=0.008, control vs 10 mM metformin p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from the C. elegans experiments with heat-inactivated bacteria, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: siRNA-mediated knock-down of arc-1, the C.elegans MID1 homolog, leads to a reduction of inclusion bodies and improved motility similar to the metformin effects.
source: siRNA-mediated knock-down of arc-1, the C.elegans MID1 homolog, leads to a reduction of inclusion bodies and improved motility similar to the metformin effects (Figure 4—figure supplement 2d and e, Figure 4—source data 1, Mann-Whitney test, p<0.0001)
evidence: This is a finding from the C. elegans RNAi experiments, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The MID1/PP2A/mTOR protein complex underlies metformin effects.
source: and confirms that the MID1/PP2A/mTOR protein complex underlies metformin effects.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the C. elegans RNAi experiments.

claim: Metformin treatment did not affect the density of OGB-1 stained cells.
source: Metformin treatment did not affect the density of OGB-1 stained cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b, Figure 5—source data 1, WT: 1413 ± 74 cells/mm2 (n = 11 mice), Hdh150: 1456 ± 90 cells/mm2 (n = 10 mice), WT met: 1351 ± 65 cells/mm2 (n = 9 mice) and Hdh150 met: 1448 ± 60 cells/ mm2 (n = 6 mice), unpaired t-test, not significant, see Table 1 for p-values).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo imaging experiments with metformin treatment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: 3 weeks of metformin treatment in the drinking water completely restored the proportion of active cells in Hdh150 mice.
source: Notably, 3 weeks of metformin treatment in the drinking water completely restored the proportion of active cells (Figure 5b, Figure 5—source data 1, Hdh150: 77.2 ± 3.5% (n = 6 mice), Hdh150 met: 64.4 ± 4.1% (n = 6 mice), Mann-Whitney test p<0.05)
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo imaging experiments with metformin treatment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: 3 weeks of metformin treatment in the drinking water completely restored the average frequency of Ca2+ transients in Hdh150 mice.
source: and the average frequency of Ca2+ transients (Figure 5a,c, Figure 5—source data 1, Hdh150: 1.2 ± 0.1 trans/min (n = 6 mice), Hdh150 met: 0.7 ± 0.06% (n = 6 mice), Mann-Whitney test p<0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo imaging experiments with metformin treatment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The individual traces of treated Hdh150 animals were indistinguishable from untreated WT animals.
source: The individual traces of treated Hdh150 animals were indistinguishable from untreated WT animals (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is an observation from the in vivo imaging experiments with metformin treatment.

claim: Metformin acts specific on dysregulated network components.
source: Importantly, in these experiments, metformin acts specific on dysregulated network components.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo imaging experiments with metformin treatment.

claim: Only the AUC of calcium transients was slightly yet significantly affected in WT mice which might be due to an increase of baseline calcium concentration induced by the activation of MID1/PP2A/mTOR signaling pathway.
source: Only the AUC of calcium transients was slightly yet significantly affected in WT mice which might be due to an increase of baseline calcium concentration induced by the activation of MID1/PP2A/mTOR signaling pathway (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo imaging experiments with metformin treatment, with a speculative explanation.

claim: Treatment with metformin in Hdh150 mice led to the complete abolishment of the hyperactive subgroup.
source: Treatment with metformin in Hdh150 mice led to the complete abolishment of the hyperactive subgroup (Figure 5d, Figure 5—source data 1, two-way ANOVA p<0.0001 and Figure 5e, Figure 5—source data 1, Chi-square test not significant, see Table 1 for p-values)
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo imaging experiments with metformin treatment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Metformin treatment restored the relative proportion of functional subgroups in Hdh150 mice.
source: and restored the relative proportion of functional subgroups.
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo imaging experiments with metformin treatment.

claim: The spatial distribution of functional subgroups remained unchanged by metformin treatment.
source: The spatial distribution of functional subgroups remained unchanged by metformin treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1f, Figure 5—source data 1, Mann-Whitney test, not significant, see Table 1 for p-values).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis with metformin treatment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Metformin treatment completely restored dysregulated microcircuit activity in Hdh150 mice.
source: This complete restoration of dysregulated microcircuit activity was also evident in the cumulative frequency distribution (Figure 5d, Figure 5—source data 1) and all other network measures found to be aberrant in young Hdh150 animals, such as synchronicity (Figure 5f and g, Figure 5—figure supplement 1d–e, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo imaging experiments with metformin treatment.

claim: Treatment with metformin fully reversed the anxiolytic behavior in Hdh150 mice.
source: Treatment with metformin fully reversed the anxiolytic behavior (Figure 5h and i, Figure 5—source data 1, Mann-Whitney test, WT vs Hdh150 p=0.002, Hdh150 vs Hdh150 met p=0.002, Hdh150 vs WT met p=0.03, WT vs Hdh150 met p=0.8).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral experiments with metformin treatment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Metformin, by interfering with the translation rate of mHtt protein, reduces protein load in cell culture and in vivo.
source: In conclusion, our data suggest that metformin, by interfering with the translation rate of mHtt protein, reduces protein load in cell culture and in vivo
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from cell culture and in vivo experiments.

claim: Metformin reverses early Huntington's disease-related network dysregulations as well as anxiety-related behavioral aberrations in mice.
source: and reverses early Huntington's disease-related network dysregulations as well as anxiety-related behavioral aberrations in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from in vivo imaging and behavioral experiments.

claim: Usage of metformin in adult C. elegans, a model of polyQ disease, significantly influences inclusion bodies formation and motility.
